The Hong Kong dollar monetary base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half of the year, standing at HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the monetary base was mainly due to the triggering of the weak-side CU in August 2018, which caused the Aggregate Balance to decline from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while Certificates of Indebtedness, circulating banknotes and coins issued by the government, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with no significant change in the Aggregate Balance since August. Subsequently, the Aggregate Balance fell slightly to around HK$70.9 billion (as of March 19) following the triggering of the weak-side CU in March. Chart 4.4 Components of the monetary base. As for broader Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators, money supply growth generally slowed in the second half of the year, partly reflecting increased macroeconomic and financial uncertainties. Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 3.6% in the first half of the year but increased only marginally by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). Hong Kong dollar deposits, a major component of M3, showed little change compared with end-June (Chart 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand and savings deposits declined, partly due to reduced investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; on the other hand, time deposits continued to grow strongly, reflecting higher deposit rates. Corresponding asset analysis shows that the slowdown in Hong Kong dollar M3 growth was driven by changes in bank capital and reserves (included in "Net Other Items"). Chart 4.5 Hong Kong dollar M3 and its corresponding asset changes. Foreign currency deposits accelerated in the second half of the year. US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half, becoming the main driver of foreign currency deposit growth, as banks attracted more deposits following increases in their US dollar preferential deposit rates (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits grew slightly by 1.4% in the second half, with renminbi deposits continuing to increase. Overall, total deposits of authorized institutions grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half of the year, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit growth. Although the Hong Kong dollar monetary base and deposit size remained substantial, HIBORs began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term HIBORs, causing them to be more volatile than longer-term HIBORs (Chart 4.7). The 3-month and 12-month HIBORs averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, about 30 basis points higher than their June averages. Moving into 2019, HIBORs generally fell as seasonal demand receded. The 3-month and 12-month HIBORs averaged 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar HIBORs. The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downward in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking movements in the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2018, the 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong government bond yields fell by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% by end-February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government bond yields, the composite interest rate, and the average new mortgage lending rate. During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost for retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit funding costs, the composite interest rate increased from 0.62% at end-June to 0.89% at end-December 2018, before falling back to 0.83% at end-January 2019 (Chart 4.8). Given the rise in funding costs, retail banks raised their best lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points following the increase in the US federal funds rate target range in September. After the US federal funds rate target range was raised again in December, retail banks did not adjust their best lending rates further. On the other hand, the average new mortgage lending rate followed the best lending rate upward, standing at around 2.45% at end-January 2019. Looking ahead, US interest rate trends, fund flows, and local financial market activities (such as new equity subscription activities) will continue to be the main drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given that the Hong Kong dollar monetary base remains substantial and the banking system holds a large amount of Exchange Fund Bills—which banks can use as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds from the Discount Window—the pace of increase in Hong Kong dollar interest rates should be moderate. Against the backdrop of escalating US-China trade frictions, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates have depreciated against the US dollar since early 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, driven by optimism over the resumption of high-level US-China trade talks, offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilized in November. Meanwhile, the spread between onshore and offshore renminbi was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates. Currently, the ongoing US-China trade frictions have not yet caused a significant impact on funding conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight offshore renminbi HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally due to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The 3-month offshore renminbi HIBOR hovered around 4% from September to December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at end-February 2019, which may reflect the recent monetary easing measures introduced by the People's Bank of China. Nevertheless, it remains to be seen how developments in US-China trade negotiations will affect liquidity in the offshore renminbi interbank market in 2019. Chart 4.10 Overnight and 3-month offshore renminbi HIBORs. The pool of offshore renminbi funds in Hong Kong expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. Renminbi customer deposits and certificate of deposit (CD) balances grew faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half, rising by 3.7% to RMB 657.7 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by renminbi customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and by 5.2% in the second half. Among these, corporate customer deposits grew faster than personal customer deposits. However, CD balances fell further by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to reduced CD issuance and a relatively large number of CDs maturing in October.

Retail banks' profitability continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017, mainly benefiting from an increase in net interest income. Capital and liquidity conditions also remained robust. Reflecting upward pressure on Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) and retail deposit rates amid the normalization of US interest rates, retail banks' overall Hong Kong dollar funding costs rose significantly, though they remained at a low level. Against a backdrop of external uncertainties, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth has shown signs of stabilization since November, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds due to continued uncertainty in US-China trade relations, a global economic slowdown, uncertainty over the pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant about the potential impact of a further deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while the return on assets rose to 1.23% from 1.14% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly driven by a substantial increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 19.4%, while the return on assets rose to 1.27% from 1.16% in 2017. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks: The net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.50% in the same period last year (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks: Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018, largely reflecting further US interest rate hikes and a decline in interbank Hong Kong dollar liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side convertibility undertaking in August 2018. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). As banks generally raised time deposit rates to secure long-term stable funding, Hong Kong dollar retail deposit rates also increased during the review period. Furthermore, following the US interest rate hike decision at the end of September, banks increased their best lending rates and raised their savings deposit rates accordingly. Given that both wholesale and retail funding costs increased, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) rose from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, though it remained at a low level by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates: (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to trend upward. In the second half of 2018, banks' average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs rose by 36 basis points, following an increase of 40 basis points in the first half (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Funding costs and tenors of licensed banks: The cumulative increase in HIBOR exceeded the rise in banks' overall funding costs, which could have a positive impact on retail banks' mortgage loans pegged to HIBOR—a product that the industry has actively promoted in recent years. However, future NIM improvements may become more limited, as most HIBOR-pegged mortgage loans have already reached their cap relative to the best lending rate (BLR). Given the uncertainty over the timing of future BLR increases, the continued upward trend in banks' funding costs amid US interest rate normalization could put pressure on overall NIMs. Looking ahead, heightened external uncertainties could cloud banks' profitability outlook. In particular, continued uncertainty in US-China trade relations, against a backdrop of slowing global economic growth, could dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. If this situation leads to a significant decline in loans and a deterioration in asset quality, it could weigh on banks' profitability. The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remains strong, well above international minimum standards. As of the end of 2018, the aggregate capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions further increased to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also rose to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capital of locally incorporated authorized institutions: 1. Aggregate position. 2. From 1 January 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions are required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement came into effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a prudent level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions: As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average LCR for Category 1 institutions rose from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio for Category 2 institutions also rose from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio: 1. Aggregate position. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicates that authorized institutions' funding positions are stable. The average NSFR for Category 1 institutions remained high at 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average core funding ratio for Category 2A institutions remained high at 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding position of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio: Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the banking system's stable funding structure. At the end of 2018, the proportion of customer deposits to total liabilities of all authorized institutions rose slightly from 54.5% six months earlier to 55.7% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions: 1. Due to rounding, figures may not add up to the total. 2. Figures represent percentages of total liabilities (including capital and reserves). 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As total loans and advances declined in the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased, the loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions in all currencies fell from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 to 72.6% at the end of the year (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions fell from 65.2% to 58.3% over the same period. In contrast, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose slightly from 85.4% at the end of June 2018 to 86.9% at the end of the year, as Hong Kong dollar deposit growth lagged far behind that of Hong Kong dollar loans. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions: The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks declined slightly in the second half of 2018. We estimate that, under a shock scenario of a parallel increase in interest rates of 200 basis points, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate position of locally incorporated licensed banks would amount to 2.44% of their total capital base at the end of 2018 (Chart 5.11). Nevertheless, given the uncertainty over the pace of further US interest rate hikes, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.11 Impact of interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks: 1. An interest rate shock refers to the impact of a standard 200 basis point parallel shock on an institution's interest rate risk exposure. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the effect on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of the bank's total capital base. Against a backdrop of continued uncertainty in US-China trade tensions, tightening global financial liquidity, and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed significantly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth has shown signs of stabilization since November 2018. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions fell by 0.9% in the second half of 2018, following an increase of 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). This decline was due to slower growth in local loans (including loans and trade finance used in Hong Kong) and a decrease in loans used outside Hong Kong. Local loan growth slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans used outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2%, respectively, in the previous six months. For 2018 as a whole, the growth rate of total loans slowed significantly to 4.4% from 16.1% in 2017. Chart 5.12 Loan growth: Looking ahead, credit demand is likely to remain weak in the short term. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) "Credit Conditions Survey" in December 2018 showed that 82% of all surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, while the proportion of authorized institutions expecting a decline in demand rose to 18% (Table 5.A). Despite a slight decline in total loans in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound. The total classified loan ratio and the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions fell slightly to 0.55% and 0.36%, respectively, at the end of December 2018, compared with 0.61% and 0.40%, respectively, at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the total classified loan ratio fell slightly to 0.50%, while the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans rose slightly to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios are at low levels by historical standards. Chart 5.13 Asset quality of retail banks: 1. Classified loans refer to loans classified as "substandard," "doubtful," or "loss." 2. Figures prior to December 2015 reflect the situation of retail banks' Hong Kong offices and overseas branches. From December 2015 onwards, the coverage of the figures was extended to include major overseas subsidiaries of retail banks. On a half-yearly basis, personal loan growth slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to slower growth in personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal loans), which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong's nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew at a slower pace than personal loan growth, the ratio of household debt to GDP rose slightly from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus pandemic, which erupted in early 2020, simultaneously impacted both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from those of previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to mitigate the economic shock caused by the pandemic, financial markets remain volatile, and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and local environments, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets have continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance stable, and total deposits growing modestly, no significant outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. After a modest rebound in the first half of 2019, total loan growth slowed in the second half of the year. The residential property market has been broadly softening since mid-2019, though the trend has been somewhat volatile. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth has shown tentative signs of stabilisation, supported by increased monetary easing by major central banks, a relaxation of US-China trade tensions, and a reduction in the risk of a "no-deal" Brexit. However, since late January, the rising number of coronavirus infections worldwide has heightened market concerns and triggered significant volatility in global financial markets. To address the evolving risks of the pandemic, several major central banks have substantially cut interest rates and expanded liquidity facilities, while some governments have introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financial conditions have tightened amid widening credit spreads and sharp declines in equity markets. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus pandemic will dampen global economic activity, with the severity of the impact depending on the pandemic's intensity and duration. In the medium term, relations between the United States and its major trading partners may once again become strained, and trade negotiations between the United Kingdom and the European Union following Brexit could prove challenging. Weak global demand continues to weigh on economic growth in East Asia. Exports from the region to major destinations, including the United States, European economies, and mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019. While some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported earnings growth, it remains to be seen whether the tech product cycle will rebound broadly. Financial markets reacted positively to the announcement of the US-China Phase One trade agreement in December 2019, and the trade truce has reduced global trade uncertainties to some extent. Nonetheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds from weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage ratios. At the same time, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may face further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by several economies in the region could adversely affect Asia's tourism industry, particularly in economies more reliant on tourism service exports. Given the region's close integration with mainland China's supply chains, manufacturing may also be impacted by the pandemic. In mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between the US and China helps reduce external uncertainties facing the mainland economy, downside pressures remain amid the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing, and a global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 identified economic stabilisation as a priority for 2020, while also emphasising financial risk control. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that mainland China's economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, especially small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have suggested that private industrial enterprises may have experienced a decline in shareholders' equity in recent years, which is viewed as a sign of "retrogression" in the private sector. Box 2 examines the drivers of changes in industrial enterprises' equity using 2018 listed company data and finds that private or smaller enterprises are not inherently more prone to contraction or "retrogression." While negative profitability was found to be the primary driver, other factors, particularly structural ones, are also noteworthy (see Box 2 for details). Economic activity in Hong Kong contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP has declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy has entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year of 2019, a sharp contrast to the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since 2009. Weakening domestic demand, particularly a decline in private consumption, was the main factor dragging down GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely impacted consumption activities, leading to a weak economic outlook and thereby reducing consumer and business confidence. Amid renewed escalation of US-China trade frictions, a slowdown in global economic growth, and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish. Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the government introduced multiple rounds of stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To provide banks with greater capacity to support the local economy and help mitigate cyclical downturns, the HKMA announced on October 14 that it would lower the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200–300 billion in lending capacity to businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, and the pandemic has recently introduced significant downside risks. As retail, accommodation, food services, tourism, and transportation sectors have yet to recover from the disruption caused by social incidents, the pandemic will deliver a double blow to these industries. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget, including one-off cash disbursements to adult permanent residents and special low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme, can provide relief to households and businesses, especially SMEs. On March 16, 2020, the HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, providing banks with greater capacity to support the local economy, particularly industries and individuals facing heightened short-term pressure due to the pandemic. In terms of GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumption and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects reach completion. Regarding external factors, the Phase One trade agreement between the US and China is expected to have a modest positive impact on the local economy in the short term. However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak could disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activities, such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2020 will range from -1.5% to 0.5%, while growth forecasts from international institutions and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slowing global economic growth, US-China trade relations, mainland China's economic performance, and local social incidents. The labour market faced increased pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising, and the real wage index falling year-on-year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of social incidents and the pandemic on the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors. Looking ahead, the unemployment rate is expected to rise further given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak. Box 3 will explore recent labour market developments and short-term prospects in greater detail. Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, primarily driven by rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually slowed. Given weak economic conditions, stabilising private residential rents, and moderate import inflation, inflation is expected to ease in the near term. Market consensus forecasts that the overall inflation rate in 2020 will range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the government forecasts the underlying inflation rate to be 2.5%. Supported by increased Hong Kong dollar demand related to equity activities, including initial public offerings (IPOs), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October 2019. In December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate intensified further, partly due to robust IPO activity and partly due to short covering in Hong Kong dollar short positions as liquidity tightened toward year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened slightly toward the end of February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly during the review period, and the Linked Exchange Rate system was not triggered. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates (HIBOR) have exhibited volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities such as IPOs. Box 4 examines how market expectations of future IPO activity affect the 3-month Hong Kong dollar HIBOR. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks' continued adjustment of deposit rates to attract funding. As some banks raised the upper limits of rates pegged to the Best Lending Rate, the average mortgage lending rate for new loans rose to around 2.6% in October. However, as the Best Lending Rate in the market was lowered from November, the average mortgage lending rate for new loans fell slightly to around 2.5% by January 2020. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance stable, and total deposits growing modestly, no significant outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. Nevertheless, we need to monitor the impact of any further deterioration in the coronavirus pandemic amid an uncertain external environment. Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to address capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. During the review period, market expectations of a US-China trade agreement led to a strengthening of both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates, but they have faced downward pressure since late January 2020 due to the coronavirus outbreak. In late 2019, the offshore renminbi traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi; this discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020 but remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool rebounded slightly after a modest decline in the previous review period. As of the end of January 2020, renminbi customer deposits and certificate of deposit balances had increased to RMB 637.4 billion. Other renminbi businesses in Hong Kong also grew, with renminbi bank loans and trade settlement activities recording strong expansion. The daily average transaction volume of the Renminbi Real-time Gross Settlement (RMB RTGS) system remained high at RMB 1.1339 trillion for the full year of 2019. Despite external uncertainties, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of mainland China's capital account, increased allocation of renminbi assets by international investors, and deepened regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives.

At the end of 2019, signs of stabilisation in global economic activity raised market expectations of a global recovery. However, since late January 2020, the surge in coronavirus infections worldwide has dashed hopes of a recovery, deepening investors' concerns about a global recession and triggering a sell-off across global financial markets. To address the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March. Given the spread of the pandemic, downside risks to the global growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 has clouded the prospects for economies in the region. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on regional growth in the short term, with the tourism sector being particularly hard hit. On the other hand, East Asia continues to face challenges from weak corporate earnings and high leverage in the private sector. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between the United States and China helps to temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downside pressures remain amid the impact of the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and a global slowdown. Monetary and fiscal policy responses by the authorities will provide some buffer. Amid continued trade tensions and policy uncertainty, manufacturing and investment remained weak, leaving global growth lacklustre in the second half of 2019. However, economic growth showed preliminary signs of stabilisation in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from earlier easing by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as a easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the US–China Phase One trade agreement. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index. However, since late January, the surge in coronavirus cases worldwide and the subsequent economic shock have heightened market concerns, triggering a sell-off across global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major export destination and plays a key role in global supply chains, disruptions to production activities and a slowdown in its economic growth due to the pandemic will have significant spillover effects and could affect the global economy (Chart 2.3). Since late February, a sharp increase in coronavirus cases outside Mainland China may exacerbate supply chain disruptions and pose a direct risk to local economic activity. Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Aggregate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread; Chart 2.3 Exports of goods and services to Mainland China by selected major advanced economies in 2018 (as a percentage of GDP). To address the potentially severe economic impact of the pandemic, some central banks (including the Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) cut interest rates since early March, while some governments introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets still face significant selling pressure, leading to a notable tightening of global financial conditions, which could further exacerbate downside pressures on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Financial Conditions Index for Advanced Economies. In addition to pandemic developments, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have subsided following the US–China Phase One trade agreement, subsequent negotiations may prove challenging as many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the European Union and the United Kingdom are expected to be difficult, sustaining Brexit-related uncertainties. Moreover, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019 due to sluggish global demand. Exports from East Asia to major destinations, including the United States, Europe, and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there are preliminary signs that the downturn in the region's technology products cycle may be bottoming out—including reports from major regional electronics firms of improved earnings at the end of 2019—it remains to be seen whether technology product exports will experience a substantive rebound. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise exports to major destinations. Weakening economic growth and trade uncertainties have also weighed on investor sentiment, with fixed capital investment in most East Asian economies falling in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which could affect the region's potential growth in the long run. To support economic growth in a low-inflation environment, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea cut policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after doing so in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross fixed capital formation. The coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may face further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Since several regional economies have imposed entry restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism sector has been hit first, with economies more reliant on Chinese visitors and tourism service exports being particularly affected by the outbreak (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and intensified pandemic would also affect regional supply chains closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism exports and Chinese visitors. In the short term, the outbreak will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects may be temporary, but the actual outcome will depend on the severity and spread of the pandemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain it. At the same time, East Asian economies face multiple headwinds. First, although markets expect corporate earnings to deteriorate in the short term (Chart 2.8), the globally accommodative monetary environment has encouraged yield-seeking behaviour, pushing asset prices higher without fundamental support. Consequently, regional equity markets are more vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of benchmark stock index constituents. Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it harder for private entities in the region to service their debts. While lower domestic interest rates can provide relief for indebted firms and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Additionally, as discussed in Special Feature 1, the risk of a build-up of private sector debt may intensify as more index-tracking funds flow into regional financial markets, although this impact may be limited to financially stronger firms and their long-term borrowing. Third, regarding external factors, East Asian economies may face increased risks from increasingly protectionist US trade policies. Despite recent progress in the US–China Phase One trade agreement, US–China trade tensions persist as fundamental trade issues between the two countries remain unresolved. The growing trade surpluses that many regional economies run with the United States (Chart 2.9) suggest that multinational corporations may continue to seek alternative sourcing routes outside China-centric supply chains to avoid tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine Asian emerging economies (excluding China) with the United States had risen to about US$167 billion. If trade surpluses with the United States continue to expand, the relevant Asian economies may become the next target of the trade war; for example, the US government imposed a hefty 456% tariff on Vietnamese steel imports in July 2019. Given this, despite the US–China trade truce, the region's trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Merchandise trade surplus with the United States. Over the past decade, the deepening integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that index-driven funds account for as much as 70% of these cross-border investment flows. Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly known as passive funds) but also actively managed funds that use indices as benchmarks. By bringing in overseas investors that relevant economies might not otherwise attract or reach, these funds help develop the financial markets of emerging market economies. Consequently, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, supporting long-term market growth and stability. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, there are market concerns that such fund investments may weaken the fiscal discipline of corporate bond issuers, leading to higher leverage levels for the relevant firms. Furthermore, some argue that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has heightened the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies—which are already sensitive to global factors and influenced by other common drivers—even more vulnerable. This special feature assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investments to relevant bonds according to the weights of constituent bonds within the index. Therefore, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions of passive bond funds may reduce the incentive for index constituent bond issuers to act in the best interests of fund investors. Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour may encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and solvency risks to the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies. Using the weights of firms from various emerging market economies in a major index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as a proxy for the extent to which their bonds are held by passive bond funds, we find that an increase in such investments raises the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated impact. In addition to fostering the development of emerging market corporate bond markets, the expanded long-term investor base resulting from passive bond funds also benefits emerging market corporate issuers. We also find that the above effect is significant only for emerging market corporate issuers with stronger fundamentals, particularly those with better solvency and lower leverage (solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged or less solvent firms do not appear to fall further into a debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investment. In summary, the above research indicates that the growth of passive bond fund investment does not necessarily significantly increase solvency risks for the corporate sectors of emerging market economies.

Due to weaker private consumption, reduced investment spending, and poor export performance, Hong Kong's economy contracted in the second half of 2019, entering its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the coronavirus outbreak has recently introduced substantial downside risks. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slower global economic growth, US-China trade relations, economic performance in Mainland China, and developments in local social events. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressure is expected to ease, although the outlook remains subject to both upside and downside risks. Hong Kong's economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP shrank by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters, respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half of the year, full-year GDP contracted by 1.2%, contrasting with the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018 and marking the first annual contraction since the 2009 global financial crisis. Chart 3.1: Real GDP growth rate and contribution by major expenditure component. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed significantly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the second, third, and fourth quarters, respectively, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the primary drag on GDP in the third quarter. Local social events severely impacted consumption activities, weakening the economic outlook and dampening consumer confidence, causing private consumption to contract significantly from the third quarter onward.33 Amid heightened economic uncertainty and deteriorating business sentiment, total investment spending remained weak and weighed on GDP in the fourth quarter.34 Externally, Hong Kong's external trade performance continued to be sluggish amid escalating US-China trade frictions, weaker global economic growth, and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals (Chart 3.2).35 Net exports weighed on GDP in the third quarter but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance, as service exports contracted sharply. Chart 3.2: Real exports and imports. Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on citizens, safeguard employment, and support businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and severely affected sectors such as retail, food services, transportation, and tourism.36 To provide banks with greater capacity to support the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) announced on October 14 that it would lower the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200–300 billion in lending capacity to businesses, including SMEs. Economic performance in Hong Kong in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the outbreak has recently introduced substantial downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruption caused by social events, the outbreak will deliver a double blow to these industries. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget, including one-off cash payments to adult permanent residents and special low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme, can provide assistance to households and businesses, especially SMEs.37 The HKMA further lowered the CCyB ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on March 16, 2020, giving banks greater capacity to support the local economy, particularly sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure due to the outbreak. In terms of GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumption and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects reach completion. Regarding external factors, the Phase One US-China trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term.38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak could disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby limiting Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2020 will range from -1.5% to 0.5%, while the average growth forecast from international and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks outlined in previous chapters. The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and the beginning of 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019 and further increased to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). Notably, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors rose to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of social events.39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline, reaching 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was primarily concentrated in the import/export, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services, and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, given the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labor market will continue to face further challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to rise further. Special Topic 3 will explore recent developments and short-term prospects in the labor market in greater detail. Chart 3.3: Labor market conditions. Local inflationary pressure continued to build up through the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually slowed. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) rose by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the increase moderating slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The underlying inflation rate, measured on a 3-month annualized basis, also eased from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflationary momentum was due to reduced price pressures across several components of the CCPI. For tradable goods, fresh pork price increases kept basic food inflation significant, although price pressures for consumer items such as clothing and footwear, as well as durable goods, remained moderate. For services, as growth in newly signed private residential rents slowed, the growth of the rental component in the CCPI also showed a downward trend (Chart 3.5). Labor cost pressure rose slightly but remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4: Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation; Chart 3.5: Rental component of the CCPI and market rents; Chart 3.6: Unit labor cost. Local inflationary pressure is expected to ease in the short term. Domestically, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential rents continue to moderate, the housing rent component of inflation should ease further. Externally, given weak global economic growth and soft energy prices, import inflation is expected to remain moderate. The market consensus forecasts that overall inflation in 2020 will range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 2.5% and the overall inflation rate at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risk factors. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economic downturn proves more severe than expected (for example, due to a prolonged coronavirus outbreak), it could further suppress inflation. On the other hand, if disruptions to fresh pork supply become more severe, this would exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the significant slowdown in Hong Kong's economy, the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8–2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. It was only as social events persisted that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% by the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus outbreak, the labor market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this special topic analyzes recent developments and short-term prospects in the labor market, including why the overall labor market remained broadly stable (with little change in the unemployment rate) in the first three quarters of 2019 and what implications this holds for future developments. This article also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, partly because adjusting labor demand entails costs, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate typically lags behind the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature helps explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% even as real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1: Real GDP growth rate and unemployment rate. Regarding labor demand, although US-China trade tensions and local social events severely impacted employment in trade- and retail- and tourism-related sectors, some major industries were able to support the overall labor market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social, and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting declines in employment in trade and retail (Chart B3.2). Despite the recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained robust, and financial activities such as fintech development and new stock listings were very active. These factors may have helped support employment in the financial and business services sectors. Additionally, public administration, social, and personal services—including education, healthcare, and social work activities—appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, the response of public administration, social, and personal services to the economic cycle is more neutral. In other words, even if the economy slows, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical factors. Chart B3.2: Changes in employment by sector in 2019. Regarding labor supply, the labor force participation rate40 fell from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against rising unemployment. Chart B3.3 shows the various demand and supply factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown, the labor force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019.41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted significantly in the second half of the year, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment fell during the recession, the lower labor force participation rate helped mitigate upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3: Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate. Some changes in labor market structure are also worth noting. In particular, an increase in the proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the proportion of self-employed and underemployed persons in total employment has fallen to 6% and 1%, respectively, in recent years, while the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group in the total employed population (around 7% in 2017).42 Therefore, companies may be able to retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time staff. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to around 44 hours currently, partly reflecting the fact that there are now more part-time workers in the employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, with upward momentum further intensifying in December, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain in the strong-side band of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS) over recent months. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was partly driven by stock-related demand and partly by short covering of Hong Kong dollar short positions amid tightening liquidity toward year-end. Overall, the Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. Although uncertainties in the external environment and market sentiment swings triggered by the coronavirus pandemic could lead to heightened fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding pressures from capital outflows without compromising its financial stability. Supported by increased stock-related demand for Hong Kong dollars (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened since mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, upward momentum further intensified, and from mid-December to February, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained in the strong-side band of the LERS. The appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar was partly due to active initial public offering activities and partly due to short covering of Hong Kong dollar short positions amid tightening liquidity toward year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side convertibility undertaking (CU) was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1: Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Chart 4.2: Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. The Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) broadly tracked the US dollar and rose slightly during the review period (Chart 4.3). The Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER) largely followed the movement of the NEER, as the impact on the REER from differences in inflation rates between Hong Kong and its trading partners was minimal. Chart 4.3: Nominal and real effective exchange rates. When assessing fund flows in Hong Kong, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct yet interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund movements and help assess monetary stability, particularly under the LERS. Cross-border fund flows, on the other hand, focus on the movement of funds across geographies through the Hong Kong banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong's overall financial system. These two fund-flow concepts require different monitoring indicators. Monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows requires attention to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large volume of Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for Hong Kong dollars will naturally decline, causing the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to weaken. Under the LERS, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side CU of HK$7.85 per US dollar, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars upon banks' request, thereby reducing the Aggregate Balance. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has largely remained stable, and as the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has stayed in the strong-side band of the LERS in recent months, no significant outflows from the Hong Kong dollar were observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border fund flows, total deposits in Hong Kong banks serve as a useful indicator. When there are large outflows of funds from the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a modest pace, indicating that no significant cross-border outflows occurred. The Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner, suggesting that the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on Hong Kong's monetary environment remained limited. Nevertheless, we need to closely monitor the risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak. With its ample foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to address capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite an uncertain external environment and a slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained sizable, rising by 4.0% since end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at end-January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the CU was not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained largely unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and circulating banknotes and coins issued by the government, increased steadily. Chart 4.4: Components of the monetary base. During the review period, broad Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators remained broadly stable. Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019 and then rose slightly by 0.2% in the seven months since end-June 2019. A corresponding assets analysis shows that the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 since end-June primarily reflected an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets and an expansion of the monetary base (driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and circulating banknotes and coins issued by the government) (Chart 4.5). Over the seven months since end-June, Hong Kong dollar deposits (a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3) remained largely unchanged (Chart 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow modestly, partly reflecting higher Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5: Hong Kong dollar M3 and changes in corresponding assets. Over the seven months since end-June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew modestly by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), driven mainly by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during the period. Other foreign currency deposits fell by 1.0% over the same period, with Hong Kong dollar-denominated renminbi deposits recording a slight decline. Overall, total deposits of authorized institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since end-June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong's overall broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5%, respectively, since end-June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), the figures should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6: Deposits of authorized institutions by currency; Chart 4.7: Broad money supply (M2). Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates exhibited volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly active initial public offering activities in the Hong Kong stock market. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) for overnight funds showed larger fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). During the review period, other short-term HIBORs generally rose. Large new equity listings and their subscription activities exerted significant pressure on overnight rates; as demonstrated by empirical analysis in Special Topic 4, market anticipation of future IPO activities also affects the 3-month HIBOR. This occurs when market participants estimate in advance the future subscription deadlines for large new listings and pre-position medium-term funds accordingly. Chart 4.8: Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates. As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it shifted downward, tracking the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% as of 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 50 basis points to 1.00% over the same period. Chart 4.9: Government bond yields, the composite interest rate, and the average lending rate for new mortgages. At the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, rose gradually from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020. This increase mainly reflected banks' continued upward adjustment of preferential deposit rates to attract deposits, thereby raising the weighted Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. Following the downward adjustment of the US federal funds rate target range at end-October 2019, several retail banks lowered their best lending rates by 12.5 basis points. Consequently, retail banks' best lending rates currently stand within the range of 5.00% to 5.50%. For mortgage loans, major banks raised the upper limit of rates pegged to the best lending rate for HIBOR-based mortgages, causing the average lending rate for new mortgages in October to rise to around 2.63%. Market best lending rates have fallen since November, and the average mortgage lending rate subsequently declined slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus pandemic to US economic activity and to support the US Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Fed lowered the federal funds rate target range by a total of 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). Although HIBORs will follow US dollar interest rate movements over the longer term, short-term HIBORs may be influenced by local factors that affect Hong Kong dollar demand, such as new equity listings in Hong Kong. The Aggregate Balance of the banking system has declined since April 2018, which may have increased the sensitivity of HIBORs to changes in Hong Kong dollar funding supply and demand. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance level of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet interbank payment and settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong's interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. Should liquidity tighten in the short term, banks can utilize the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Given the potential escalation of US-China trade tensions, offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi falling to a decade-low of 7.19 per US dollar on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Entering October, market expectations of a resumption of US-China trade negotiations reversed the renminbi depreciation trend; offshore and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter and, following the signing of the US-China Phase One trade agreement, briefly rose above the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020. However, since late January, the coronavirus outbreak has again exerted downward pressure on offshore and onshore renminbi. The offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of the period from May to August, at a premium for most of late 2019, and the discount briefly widened at end-January 2020; however, the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10: Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates. Despite fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the 3-month offshore renminbi HIBOR continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight offshore renminbi HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations in late August and late November due to MSCI A-share adjustments, and again at end-January 2020 near the Lunar New Year holiday.

Retail banks' profitability in Hong Kong recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019, owing to increased uncertainties in the global and local economic environment. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality stayed at healthy levels by historical standards. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed in the second half of the year, it still outpaced deposit growth over the same period. Accordingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratios (LDRs) of all authorized institutions, measured in all currencies and in Hong Kong dollars, increased. However, given that the overall balance sheet of the banking system remained stable and deposits were largely unchanged, the liquidity position of the banking sector stayed robust. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future trajectory of US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risks intensify. In the second half of 2019, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Accordingly, the return on assets (ROA) dipped marginally to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, down from 1.23% in the same period of 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks narrowed slightly to 1.63% in the second half of 2019 from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.2), their net interest income continued to record modest growth during the review period. However, increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses led to a slight decline in profitability. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks; Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks. Despite three 25-basis-point cuts to the US Federal Funds target rate in the second half of 2019, the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) wholesale funding market has not experienced significant downward pressure to date. Conversely, short-term HKD interbank offered rates (HIBORs) have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019, driven by various local factors, including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand due to large initial public offerings (IPOs), and tighter interbank market liquidity conditions. Meanwhile, longer-term HKD HIBORs remained largely stable during the review period, with the three-month HIBOR standing at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to the level six months prior (blue line in Chart 5.3). On the retail front, as HKD savings deposit rates remained near zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the US policy rate cuts. On the other hand, as HKD liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term, stable deposit funding. Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of HKD deposits, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks) rose gradually from 0.95% six months prior to 1.09% at the end of 2019, although it remained low by historical standards (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates. From a broader perspective, given that the decline in the cost of US dollar (USD) funding for locally incorporated banks offset the slight increase in their HKD funding costs, the average overall funding cost for HKD and USD combined for locally incorporated banks fell marginally by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks' net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding costs and the relatively high level of HKD HIBORs, which supported banking sector profitability over the same period. Chart 5.4 Funding costs and tenor for HKD and USD of locally incorporated banks. Note 1: Starting from June 2019, all locally incorporated banks subject to the new local "interest rate risk in the banking book" (IRRBB) framework will submit returns under the new framework, while those exempted will continue to submit returns under the existing IRRBB framework. The overall funding cost and tenor are calculated as weighted averages based on the relevant figures for these two categories of banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Looking ahead, multiple downside risk factors in the external and local environment will continue to cast a shadow over banks' profitability outlook. These include uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, the future trajectory of US-China trade relations, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could weaken already fragile global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low interest rate environment may persist, which could exert pressure on banks' future net interest margins. Locally, social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to dampen business investment and market confidence. Against an already weak economic backdrop, a continuation or further escalation of the situation could worsen the outlook for credit demand and deteriorate bank asset quality. In terms of overall market developments, the Hong Kong banking sector began to roll out virtual banking services after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) granted eight virtual banking licences. As these new market entrants may increase their market share by attracting new customers through more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates, this could put upward pressure on the funding costs of incumbent banks. While the short-term impact may remain mild given the currently limited scale of virtual banks' operations, the longer-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks accelerate the adoption of fintech to maintain competitiveness. The findings of Special Topic 5 show that the extent of fintech adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically correlated with improvements in cost efficiency and enhancements in profitability. The capital base of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above the minimum international standards. As at the end of 2019, the aggregate capital ratio of locally registered authorized institutions further increased to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also rose to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capital of locally registered authorized institutions. In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, the Basel III non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement serves to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally registered authorized institutions remained at a prudent level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally registered authorized institutions. The liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period, as measured by the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" (LCR) requirement under Basel III. The average LCR for Category 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) for Category 2 institutions also increased modestly from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also far exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio. The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), as one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicates the stability of authorized institutions' funding profiles. The average NSFR for Category 1 institutions remained high at 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average core funding ratio for Category 2A institutions stayed high at 134.5%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity and stable funding profile of authorized institutions demonstrate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure in the banking system. At the end of 2019, the proportion of customer deposits to total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained largely unchanged, falling slightly from 56.4% six months prior to 56.3% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions. The average HKD LDR of all authorized institutions rose from 89.3% at the end of June 2019 to 90.3% at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.10), as HKD loans and advances remained largely stable while deposits declined slightly during the review period. Meanwhile, the average foreign currency LDR also increased from 58.9% to 60.4% over the same period, driven by faster growth in foreign currency loans compared with deposits. Overall, the average LDR of all authorized institutions, measured in all currencies, rose from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of the year. Given that the overall balance sheet of the banking system has remained stable since April 2019 and deposits were largely unchanged, there were no apparent signs of large-scale outflows of funds from the HKD or the Hong Kong banking system during the review period. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions. The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2019. We estimate that, under a shock scenario assuming a 200-basis-point increase in both HKD and USD interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate position of locally incorporated licensed banks would amount to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11).
