Chart 5.11 Impact of HKD and USD interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks. Against the backdrop of US-China trade tensions, a global economic slowdown, and ongoing local social incidents, bank credit growth slowed in the second half of 2019 after a modest rebound in the first half. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth (measured by changes in total loans and advances of all authorized institutions) increased modestly by 4.2% in the first half of 2019, before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was due to a deceleration in both local loans (including loans and trade finance used in Hong Kong) and loans used outside Hong Kong during the review period. Local loans and loans used outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2%, respectively, in the second half of 2019, down from 4.5% and 3.5% in the first half. Nevertheless, total loan growth for 2019 as a whole still rose modestly to 6.7%, up from 4.4% for the whole of 2018.

The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines brought hope for economic reopening and boosted global growth prospects. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets repeatedly hit record highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery is expected to vary across economies. In the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, high debt levels, and the lasting scars from the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers. Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and interbank markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level against the US dollar, driven primarily by stock-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weak economic activity and subdued credit demand due to recurring pandemic outbreaks, total bank loans declined slightly in the second half of the year, although they still recorded a modest increase for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained largely stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may weaken the repayment capacity of businesses and households, and the banking sector should remain vigilant about the impact of these downside risks on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but growth slowed again from the fourth quarter as COVID-19 infection numbers rose. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development at the end of 2020, markets expected the pandemic to eventually end, which would help the global economy return to normal and accelerate growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, despite emerging signs of a disconnect with the real economy. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. It remains to be seen whether vaccines can be distributed widely. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing policies could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, prompting central banks to reduce monetary accommodation earlier than anticipated and ending market expectations of a prolonged low-interest-rate environment. In the longer term, policymakers will need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address numerous economic legacies of the pandemic, including high global debt levels and lasting economic scars. In East Asia, GDP growth in the second half of 2020 improved, supported by a rebound in export demand. Against a backdrop of increased risk appetite, inflows of portfolio investment into the region rebounded, and yield-chasing activities re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, East Asia still faces continued uncertainties stemming from the pandemic. First, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity amid global competition for vaccine procurement, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service industries. Second, variables in vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy, coupled with weakening fiscal positions in regional governments, could sour market sentiment and trigger a reversal of capital flows. As for mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. For the full year of 2020, the mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook will still depend largely on pandemic developments and changes in US-China tensions. The latest consensus forecasts show that the mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi depreciated for several months at the beginning of 2020, but then strengthened for the rest of the year as the economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened, and mainland bond markets recorded strong capital inflows. Detailed research shows that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamentals, rather than market sentiment, played a more important role in driving renminbi exchange rate fluctuations (see Box 1 for details). Hong Kong’s economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below pre-pandemic levels. As domestic demand picked up slightly and merchandise exports expanded further, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and the first time the economy had contracted for two consecutive years following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by industry show that consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracted more severely than the overall economy during the pandemic. To address the ongoing pandemic, the government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-Epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to help affected industries and citizens and enhance Hong Kong’s capacity to combat the epidemic. The government also announced additional countercyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one-off electronic consumption voucher of HK$5,000 and the provision of 100% guaranteed personal loans for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the "Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism," announced in March 2021 that the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday" scheme would be extended to October of that year and that the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme would also be extended. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. COVID-19 vaccines are expected to enable a return to normal economic activity, and the local economy is expected to resume positive growth in 2021 (for the full year). However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery will be affected by many uncertainties, including pandemic developments and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s merchandise and service exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programs. The government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2021 will be between 3.5% and 5.5%, while growth forecasts from international institutions and private sector analysts average 4.4%. The labour market situation deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and the beginning of 2021. The unemployment rate rose further, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a high since the SARS outbreak. To address the worsening labour market situation, the government launched the "Employment Support Scheme" under the second round of the Anti-Epidemic Fund, providing time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain staff. After the "Employment Support Scheme" ended, the government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off allowances) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-Epidemic Fund to further support industries severely affected by the pandemic. In the short term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Box 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell significantly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and further declined to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021, respectively. The underlying inflation rate, measured on a 3-month annualised basis and reflecting inflation momentum, has fluctuated slightly in recent months but has remained at a low level. Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are likely to remain mild in the short term, particularly as local inflation continues to be suppressed by slower growth in newly signed private residential rents. The market consensus forecast for overall inflation in 2021 is at a moderate level of 1.4%, while the government forecasts underlying and overall inflation rates of 1.0% and 1.6%, respectively, for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level against the US dollar, driven primarily by stock-related funding demand, including from robust new stock offering activities and southbound inflows via Stock Connect (Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong). Funding activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain strong. During the review period, the strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with inflows of HK$263.3 billion into the Hong Kong dollar. The strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. From a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating that there were no signs of significant outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to pandemic developments, the pace of economic recovery, and continued US-China tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong has sufficient foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding capital flow fluctuations. As the triggering of the strong-side convertibility undertaking increased the aggregate balance, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) generally remained at very low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. Due to lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. As the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate strengthened, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi exchange rate, with an average premium of about 100 basis points in the fourth quarter, which remains moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with renminbi customer deposits and certificate of deposit balances increasing to RMB 826.3 billion as of the end of January 2021. As for other renminbi businesses, Hong Kong’s renminbi bank loans decreased, while renminbi trade settlement increased, with the daily average transaction volume of the renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement System remaining high at RMB 1,191.5 billion for the full year of 2020. Hong Kong has efficient financial infrastructure that provides investors with numerous channels for cross-border capital flows linked to the mainland. As the mainland’s capital account continues to open up, international investors’ demand for renminbi assets increases, and regional economic and financial cooperation deepens under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Supported by rising global stock markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by mainland investors via Stock Connect, the Hong Kong stock market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. Global stock markets rose due to unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies; market optimism about positive progress in vaccine development, which could help accelerate the recovery of economic activity; and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered from its sharp decline in 2020, rising 15.1% during the review period, and briefly surpassed the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021, a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance volumes, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. After experiencing significant net outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence quickly recovered as governments around the world introduced unprecedented economic stimulus measures, and inflows of bond funds into the local market rebounded. Although bond yields rebounded modestly over the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remained near historic lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, markets expected the COVID-19 pandemic to eventually end, allowing the global economy to grow at an accelerated pace thereafter. Coupled with expectations of a "lower-for-longer" global monetary policy stance, investors were undeterred by a resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets reached new highs in early 2021. However, the lofty expectations of financial markets were at odds with a still-challenging macroeconomic environment; should the economic recovery fall short of expectations or policy support be withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for instance, due to higher-than-expected inflation), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers face the dilemma of determining when to withdraw policy support, while also needing to address numerous issues left in the pandemic's wake, including elevated debt levels and lasting economic scars. Persistent uncertainty surrounding the pandemic continues to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, where emerging market economies with slower development may face greater challenges in procuring and distributing vaccines. Any setbacks in vaccination programmes could reverse the current optimism and destabilise capital inflows and financial markets. In Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. Looking forward, the growth outlook remains highly uncertain, largely depending on the evolution of the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. Consequently, the government announced that it would maintain its supportive policy stance and emphasised the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the release of pent-up demand following the economic reopening, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, COVID-19 infection numbers have risen again, prompting governments worldwide to reinstate lockdown and social distancing measures, causing global growth momentum to weaken once more. At the end of 2020, the emergence of a more transmissible variant, which subsequently spread worldwide, further exacerbated the situation. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of several vaccines for use by the end of 2020, markets expected the pandemic to eventually end, allowing the global economy to return to normal and grow at an accelerated pace. Another driver supporting the global economic recovery was the continuation of policy stimulus measures, including major central banks' commitment to "lower-for-longer" monetary policies amid weak inflation, as well as ongoing fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) raised its forecast for global GDP growth in 2021 to 5.5% in January 2021, 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 projection (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF forecasts for real GDP growth in January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, with cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recovery seeing their share prices rise, driving global equity prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios for major stock indices However, while financial markets performed strongly, the macroeconomic environment remained challenging, and the disconnect between the two could lead to asset market volatility amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the pandemic under control hinges on the widespread distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, overall global vaccination rates were still low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms such as COVAX aim to promote more equitable vaccine distribution, limited vaccine supply means that low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies are likely to persist. If the pandemic is not brought under control, jurisdictions may need to maintain social distancing and other restrictions, thereby undermining the outlook for global recovery. Chart 2.3 Share of population that has received at least one dose of vaccine in selected economies (as of March 15, 2021) Second, the rebound in financial markets has been predicated on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly "lower-for-longer" monetary policies. However, there is a risk that support measures could be withdrawn at a faster pace than expected. For example, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have already risen due to a combination of supply bottlenecks, strong money and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing (Chart 2.4). If inflation proves stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back monetary easing, and higher-than-expected inflation data could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Chart 2.4 5-year/5-year forward inflation-linked swap rates for the US and the Eurozone Third, there is significant uncertainty regarding the future of US-China relations. The trend of "decoupling" between the US and China, particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hawkish stance of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the US toward Mainland China, this trend is unlikely to be reversed under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation in US-China tensions could trigger financial market volatility in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to grapple with the question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. While withdrawing these measures too early could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a "cliff effect," the long-term costs of maintaining them are high, including fiscal burdens and delays in the necessary post-pandemic reallocation of resources, such as allowing "zombie firms" whose business models are no longer viable to continue operating with government support. Additionally, policymakers must address numerous issues left in the pandemic's wake. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 due to declining corporate revenues and surging government spending (Chart 2.5). Although the problems associated with the rapid rise in debt may not be imminent given that global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, continued debt accumulation in both the public and private sectors could raise market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt as a percentage of GDP Another lingering issue concerns the potential long-term economic losses or "scarring" caused by the pandemic. For example, heightened uncertainty may lead firms to cut back on investment, while workers who remain unemployed for extended periods may permanently exit the labour market, resulting in a significant waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after a sharp decline in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The main driver of the economic recovery was a rebound in exports, with demand for electronics and technology equipment being particularly strong. Meanwhile, the hardest-hit service industries, such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face interaction with customers, continued to struggle. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020 Despite lingering uncertainty surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment funds have flowed back into the region. Since the second half of the previous year, the region has attracted more bond inflows due to improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to bonds in advanced economies (Chart 2.7). As signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production programmes were launched, equity inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Currencies in the region also appreciated in response to portfolio inflows, with the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index rebounding by about 10% from its lowest point in March of the previous year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment flows East Asia continues to face persistent uncertainty related to the pandemic. First, while the rollout of vaccines offers hope for the region's hard-hit service industries and economies, competition worldwide for early vaccine supplies has driven up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacities. Consequently, economies in the region with slower development may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination rates across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, given that investors' optimism has been largely driven by the rollout of vaccines, if vaccination progress or effectiveness falls far short of expectations, the current capital inflows and rebound in financial asset prices could come to an abrupt end. A sudden halt in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market volatility. As COVID-19 was successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovered, the Mainland Chinese economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. Meanwhile, exports also continued to grow, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products such as medical supplies and high-tech goods (Chart 2.8). For the full year of 2020, despite facing an unprecedented shock from the COVID-19 pandemic, Mainland China's GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contributions to GDP growth by demand component Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts indicate that the Mainland Chinese economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be a major driver of economic growth. However, the sustainability of the recovery will still depend, to some extent, on the evolution of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the Mainland have returned to normal, the services sector continues to face some disruption as several northern provinces have experienced renewed outbreaks. Externally, while exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to renewed outbreaks in most developed economies. Additionally, US-China tensions are unlikely to ease in the short term, but the earlier signing of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the agreed Comprehensive Agreement on Investment (CAI) between China and the EU will help further integrate China with other economies, potentially offsetting some of the adverse effects of US-China decoupling on the economic recovery. Given that the economic outlook remains highly uncertain, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that its existing policy stance would not undergo major changes in 2021 to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. Furthermore, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. In the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan identifies technological self-reliance and the "dual circulation" strategy as priority development directions, with the aim of achieving a per capita GDP level equivalent to that of a moderately developed country by 2035. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on the repayment ability of bond-issuing enterprises appears to have been limited, with the overall default rate in the Mainland Chinese bond market remaining at a low level in the second half of 2020. However, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 due to a sharp rise in defaults by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) (Chart 2.9). While the increase in SOE defaults primarily reflects the central government's determination to break the "rigid repayment" expectation of SOEs to promote more reasonable market risk pricing, limited fiscal space for some local governments, particularly those in less developed regions, may also be a contributing factor. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Size and proportion of onshore bond defaults In the second half of 2020, financing costs for corporate issuers increased, especially for those with higher risk profiles. Although the continued economic recovery and gradual normalisation of interest rates contributed to some extent to the rise in financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate default events in the final quarter of 2020 caused credit spreads to widen significantly (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields In the property market, Mainland Chinese housing prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. In contrast, price growth in lower-tier cities was much slower (Chart 2.11). Meanwhile, the problem of oversupply in third-tier cities that plagued them in previous years was largely brought under control in 2020, partly due to strong sales in these cities amid buoyant market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities stood at around 13 months, well below the peak of 31 months recorded in early 2015.

Although real GDP remained well below pre‑pandemic levels, Hong Kong’s economy improved in the second half of 2020 as domestic demand picked up and merchandise exports expanded further. With expectations that COVID‑19 vaccination would allow economic activity to return to normal, the local economy was poised to resume growth in 2021 after recording its deepest contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including pandemic developments and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. Accordingly, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while local inflation pressure should stay mild. Hong Kong’s economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained far below pre‑pandemic levels. On a year‑on‑year basis, the decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest drop on record and the first time the economy contracted for two consecutive years following a 1.2% decline in 2019. The latest GDP data by industry also show that economic activity in the vast majority of sectors recorded year‑on‑year declines in recent quarters, with consumption‑ and tourism‑related industries performing worse than the overall economy. On a quarter‑on‑quarter basis, real GDP began to recover in the third quarter of 2020, ending a five‑quarter consecutive decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Local private consumption returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters, but consumer confidence remained weak as authorities re‑imposed social distancing measures amid the third and fourth waves of the pandemic locally. Overall investment spending also increased in the second half of the year as business sentiment improved temporarily. Hong Kong’s merchandise trade expanded further, partly benefiting from stronger export performance, especially to Mainland China (Chart 3.2). Trade in services remained weak, as the global tourism industry stayed stagnant. Overall, net exports (the trade surplus) subtracted from GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting that the rebound in merchandise exports was slower than that in imports. To address the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti‑Epidemic Fund, totalling HK$30.4 billion, between September and December 2020 to assist pandemic‑affected sectors and individuals and to enhance Hong Kong’s capacity to combat the epidemic. The Government also announced further counter‑cyclical measures in the latest 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one‑off electronic consumption voucher of HK$5,000 and the provision of 100%‑guaranteed personal loans for the unemployed. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with the “Banking Sector SME Loan Coordination Mechanism,” announced in March 2021 that the “Pre‑approved Principal Payment Holiday” scheme would be extended until October of that year, and that the repayment period for trade‑finance loans under the scheme would also be extended. These extensions are expected to help alleviate cash‑flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID‑19 vaccines expected to enable a return to normal economic activity, Hong Kong’s economy is projected to resume positive growth in 2021 (for the year as a whole), though the strength and pace of the recovery remain subject to numerous uncertainties, including pandemic developments and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s merchandise and services exports, while the recovery pace in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large‑scale vaccination programmes, thereby affecting Hong Kong’s merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts that real GDP will grow by 3.5%–5.5% in 2021, while the average growth forecast from international and private‑sector analysts is 4.4%. Labour‑market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and in early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, a 17‑year high (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, a high since the SARS outbreak. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low point (Chart 3.3), while government data show that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The nominal average wage index, which reflects labour income, slowed to 2.0% year‑on‑year in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. To address the worsening labour‑market situation, the Government introduced the “Employment Support Scheme” under the second round of the Anti‑Epidemic Fund, providing time‑limited (June–November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain staff. After the scheme ended, the Government launched other targeted measures (such as one‑off allowances) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti‑Epidemic Fund to further support hard‑hit sectors. In the short term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Special Topic 2 examines the potential impact of the boom and bust in inbound tourism on the local labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour‑market conditions; Chart 3.4 Different indicators of consumer‑price inflation. Local inflation pressure continued to ease over the eight months from mid‑2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer‑price inflation rate fell significantly to 0.3% and 0.2% year‑on‑year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and dropped further to –0.5% and –0.1% in January and February 2021 (Chart 3.4). The 3‑month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also remained low despite some volatility in recent months. In particular, price pressure for basic foodstuffs eased, and the cost of dining out fell markedly, reflecting that more restaurants offered delivery discounts while dine‑in services were restricted. Price pressure for other traded goods, such as durables, remained moderate. On the services side, the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index stayed weak as private residential rents stabilised (Chart 3.5). Labour‑cost pressure also eased in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.5 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents; Chart 3.6 Unit labour cost. Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, local inflation pressure should stay mild in the near term. In particular, local inflation will continue to be contained, partly due to slower growth in newly signed private residential leases. The market consensus forecasts that overall inflation in 2021 will be moderate at 1.4%, while the Government projects underlying inflation of 1% and overall inflation of 1.6% for 2021. As the COVID‑19 pandemic took hold, inbound tourism quickly collapsed, raising concerns that the crisis could have scarring effects on the future recovery of the labour market. This special topic therefore provides an empirical analysis of the impact of a boom in inbound tourism on the local labour market, in order to explore the potential effects of the current tourism downturn. Since 2000, inbound tourism has experienced large fluctuations (Chart B2.1). In particular, visitor arrivals fell during the 2003 SARS outbreak. After the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) was launched in July of that year, visitor numbers began to surge. Under the original IVS, Mainland residents could apply individually for one to two visits per year, each stay not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded in April 2009 to allow eligible residents holding Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple‑entry “Individual Visit” visas (allowing multiple visits on a single visa). Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased substantially. Driven by new cross‑boundary infrastructure linking the Mainland, visitor arrivals reached a historic high in late 2018 to early 2019. Subsequently, local social events caused visitor numbers in the second half of 2019 to halve, and inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020 due to the COVID‑19 pandemic. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies. We use the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as a case study to examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and earnings. We treat the IVS launched in 2003 as a quasi‑random economic shock because its introduction was largely exogenous in timing and could not have been anticipated by Hong Kong residents. Our main analysis draws on population data from the Hong Kong Population Census or By‑census. Specifically, we use the 5% sample from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Censuses or By‑censuses. In addition, we define tourism‑related industries as catering, retail, hotels and transportation. First, we adopt a “difference‑in‑differences” framework to compare differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between a “treatment group” of younger workers (aged 20–40) and a “control group” of older workers (aged 41–65). We assign the younger cohort to the treatment group because they are still at an early stage of their careers and can adjust their employment choices more flexibly in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. Since the impact of the tourism boom on the labour market may vary over time, we also employ an “event‑study” approach to identify time‑varying effects. Our empirical results show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers (especially women and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism‑related industries after the IVS was implemented. In particular, the IVS had a significant and persistent impact on the probability of young women entering tourism‑related industries, remaining at around 5 percentage points (relative to the average difference in entry probability for the older cohort) since 2006 (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar approach to compare earnings between those employed in tourism‑related industries (treatment group) and those in non‑tourism‑related industries (control group). The estimation results indicate that, after the IVS was implemented, workers in tourism‑related industries experienced higher earnings growth than employees in non‑tourism‑related industries. Furthermore, compared with similar employees in other sectors, female workers and those with lower educational attainment in tourism‑related industries saw larger and increasing earnings gains (3–20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment; Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on earnings of female and low‑education workers. These findings are broadly consistent with international experience, highlighting that tourism is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women and workers with lower educational attainment. In the case of Hong Kong, our results also align with previous analyses, which showed that strong growth in inbound tourism increased demand for lower‑skill workers and improved the robustness of the lower‑skill labour market. As inbound tourism moves from boom to bust, these worker groups may be more adversely affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained close to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level, which was triggered on multiple occasions between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was primarily driven by equity-related funding needs, including those arising from robust new share issuance activities and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance rose to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) fell across the board. Although uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued tensions in US-China relations may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand pressures arising from such volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has stayed close to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related funding needs, including those from robust new share issuance activities and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some of the proceeds from initial public offerings (IPOs) were repatriated, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate fluctuated within a narrow band of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December, owing to an improvement in market sentiment in the local stock market and expectations of rising funding demand toward year-end. As fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on February 26, 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, which reflected substantial capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered 47 times. Under the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, causing the Aggregate Balance to rise from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered 85 times in 2020 as a whole, resulting in cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of large-scale outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures show that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any abnormal capital movements. Chart 4.1: Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Chart 4.2: Equity funds raised on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK); Chart 4.3: Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar's nominal effective exchange rate index generally declined, tracking the weakness of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). Given the very small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate index, the latter moved largely in line with the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4: Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued tensions in US-China relations may exacerbate capital flow volatility. As an international financial center, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities (such as new share issuance), resulting in substantial capital inflows and outflows. On the one hand, such fundraising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently flow out of Hong Kong to meet business needs. Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability. Amid continued inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). By component, the increase in the monetary base during this period reflected the rise in the Aggregate Balance resulting from multiple triggers of the strong-side convertibility undertaking. Meanwhile, other components—including Certificates of Indebtedness, circulating banknotes and coins issued by the government, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes—remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5: Components of the monetary base. During the review period, large-scale new share issuance activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, causing Hong Kong dollar broad money (M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component to rise significantly between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). As new share issuance activities concluded and customers repaid IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels by the end of 2020. In January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased again substantially, mainly driven by large-scale new share issuance activities at the end of the month. Overall, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7% over the seven months since the end of June; excluding the impact of the new share issuance activities at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew moderately by 9.1%. Based on the corresponding assets analysis, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was primarily driven by the increase in the monetary base resulting from triggers of the strong-side convertibility undertaking (Chart 4.7). As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period; excluding the impact of the new share issuance activities at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits declined due to low deposit rates, this was fully offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits, partly driven by investment demand. Chart 4.6: Deposits of authorized institutions by currency; Chart 4.7: Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and corresponding assets. Overall foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven months since the end of June. US dollar deposits fell slightly by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, total deposits of authorized institutions rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period, owing to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by new share issuance activities (Chart 4.6). Excluding the new share issuance activities at the end of January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal funding demand related to IPOs and business and investment-related activities); therefore, the statistics should be interpreted with caution. As the Aggregate Balance increased, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) generally remained at very low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large-scale new share issuance activities in the second half of 2020, HIBOR did not experience significant volatility, owing to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8: Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates. The Hong Kong dollar yield curve largely followed the trend of the US dollar yield curve, becoming steeper during the review period as short-term bond yields fell while long-term bond yields rose (Chart 4.9). Compared with the end of June, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell slightly by 4 basis points to 0.23% at the end of February, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9: Government bond yields, composite interest rate, and average new mortgage lending rate. Hong Kong dollar interest rates at the retail level mainly followed the decline in Hong Kong dollar HIBOR. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% at the end of February 2021 (Chart 4.9). Owing to lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, largely tracking the movement of the 1-month Hong Kong dollar HIBOR. Meanwhile, the best lending rates offered by retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low interest rate environment in the United States, Hong Kong dollar interest rates should remain low, with occasional fluctuations driven by capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide sufficient buffer to maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar have strengthened since the end of May (Chart 4.10), largely reflecting better economic prospects in mainland China compared with other parts of the world, as well as US dollar weakness. FTSE Russell's announcement in late September that it would include mainland government bonds in the World Government Bond Index further supported renminbi strength through investment demand. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi exchange rate, averaging around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remains moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10: Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates. During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight offshore renminbi HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand toward year-end, it stayed below 4% for most of the time (Chart 4.11). The 3-month offshore renminbi HIBOR followed onshore renminbi rates in falling in late December, then rose again in late January, partly due to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11: Overnight and 3-month offshore renminbi HIBOR. In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi funding pool continued to expand. Since the fourth quarter, renminbi deposit growth has accelerated, partly reflecting renminbi appreciation and higher renminbi interest rates relative to other currencies. Compared with the end of June 2020, the growth rate of renminbi customer deposits and Certificates of Deposit (CDs) accelerated, reaching RMB 826.3 billion at the end of January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Of this, renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. Meanwhile, CD balances fell by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12: Renminbi deposits and CDs in Hong Kong. As for other renminbi businesses, renminbi loan balances fell by 2.4% to RMB 159.2 billion over the seven months since the end of June 2020. On the other hand, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. Over the seven months from July 2020 to January 2021, the transaction volume handled by local banks reached RMB 3,769.5 billion, an increase of 16.7% year-on-year. Among the relevant transactions, remittances from Hong Kong to the mainland grew at a faster pace than remittances from the mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong possesses a large renminbi funding pool, which is sufficient to continue supporting a high volume of renminbi payment and financial transactions. In 2020 as a whole, the daily average transaction volume of the Renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached RMB 1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB 1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Retail banks' profitability further declined in the second half of 2020 compared with the same period in 2019, owing to the prolonged economic downturn caused by recurring waves of the COVID-19 pandemic and the impact of a prolonged low interest rate environment. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust, supported by strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) decided to extend several relief measures to continue supporting the overall economy through the difficult period. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activities can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties, together with ongoing geopolitical tensions, will weigh on business activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may weaken the repayment ability of businesses and households, and the banking sector should remain vigilant about the impact of these downside risks on asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Accordingly, the return on assets (ROA) declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, from 1.13% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks narrowed to 1.01% in the second half of 2020 from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.2), resulting in a decline in net interest income that more than offset a slight increase in non-interest income, thereby leading to a drop in profitability. For 2020 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and ROA declined to 0.77% from 1.19% in 2019. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks; Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks. Hong Kong dollar (HKD) liquidity became more ample, largely due to substantial fund inflows driven by stock market activities. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the three-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points during the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks) exhibited a similar trend, falling significantly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and rate cuts on time deposits by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates. From a broader perspective, the average overall funding cost for HKD and US dollar (USD) funds of licensed banks in Hong Kong fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Funding costs and tenor of HKD and USD funds for licensed banks. Looking ahead, the profitability outlook for the banking sector remains challenging, as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist, continuing to weigh on banks' NIM performance. Moreover, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have boosted market optimism about the global economic outlook, the path of economic recovery remains highly uncertain, given that considerable uncertainties still surround vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect loan quality and profitability in the banking sector in the near term. The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remains strong and is well above international minimum standards. The aggregate capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio during the period was 18.7%, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a prudent level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, above the statutory minimum requirement of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capital of locally incorporated authorized institutions; Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions. The liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period, as measured by the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" (LCR) requirement under Basel III. The average LCR for Category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. Over the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio for Category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio. The latest figures under the "Net Stable Funding Ratio" (NSFR) requirement also indicate that authorized institutions' funding position is stable. The average NSFR for Category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio for Category 2A institutions stood at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5%, respectively, in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%, respectively. The ample liquidity and sound funding position of authorized institutions demonstrate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure in the banking system. At the end of 2020, customer deposits accounted for 56.1% of total liabilities of all authorized institutions, similar to the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions. As total deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans decreased over the same period, the average loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio of all authorized institutions in all currencies fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% at the end of 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits largely reflected growth in both HKD and foreign currency deposits. Accordingly, the average HKD LTD ratio and foreign currency LTD ratio fell to 83.5% and 61.0%, respectively, at the end of 2020, compared with 86.4% and 65.5%, respectively, six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions. The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under a stress test assuming a 200 basis point increase in HKD and USD interest rates, the estimated decline in the economic value of the interest rate position of locally incorporated licensed banks would amount to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of HKD and USD interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks. Against the backdrop of a prolonged economic downturn caused by recurring waves of the pandemic and tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances declined moderately in the second half of 2020. However, for 2020 as a whole, the banking sector's total credit still recorded positive growth, although the growth rate slowed significantly to 1.2% from 6.7% in 2019. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions grew by 3.0% in the first half of 2020 but fell by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was due to decreases in both local loans (including loans and trade finance used in Hong Kong) and loans used outside Hong Kong. In particular, total local loans fell slightly by 0.9% in the second half of the year, while total loans used outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with growth of 2.6% and 4.2%, respectively, in the previous six months. Chart 5.12 Loan growth by currency. HKD loans, after falling by 2.0% in the first half of the year, were largely maintained at a level similar to that at the end of June 2020. Foreign currency loans, after growing strongly by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, fell by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a decline in USD loan demand as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector became slightly more optimistic about the outlook for short-term credit demand compared with six months earlier. The HKMA's "Credit Conditions Survey" in December 2020 showed that the proportion of responding authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decrease over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). Loan quality deteriorated slightly as the pandemic adversely affected the repayment ability of households and companies, but it remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The aggregate classified loan ratio of all authorized institutions rose moderately to 0.9% at the end of 2020 from 0.79% six months earlier, while the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions increased to 0.57% at the end of 2020 from 0.49% at the end of June 2020. For retail banks, the aggregate classified loan ratio and the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans rose to 0.82% and 0.48%, respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, global economic performance was weak, but inflationary pressures persisted and intensified across various regions, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of a large-scale pandemic resurgence and the possibility that monetary policy tightening could exceed expectations if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than anticipated. Should the Federal Reserve tighten monetary policy substantially, leading to a tightening of global financial conditions, this would exert pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has erupted, which could have a significant impact on the global economy through trade and financial channels and further complicate the outlook for global monetary policy. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but trading remained smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately over the review period, with no significant signs of funds flowing out of the Hong Kong banking system. For the full year of 2021, the growth of total bank loans accelerated. On the other hand, the residential property market softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could threaten the sustainability of the economic recovery, and combined with the possibility that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation may be faster than expected, these risk factors will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow down in late 2021, and this weakness continued into 2022, as the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant led to increased restrictions on movement worldwide, while persistent supply bottlenecks continued to constrain production. Meanwhile, global inflationary pressures intensified amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, spreading to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Recently, the surge in commodity prices following the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility could lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, further complicating the outlook for global monetary policy. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook remains highly uncertain. In the short term, a large-scale pandemic outbreak could not be ruled out, potentially leading to the reimposition of lockdown measures and a further deterioration of supply bottlenecks. In the United States, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and broad-based than expected grows, the Federal Reserve has adopted a more hawkish stance, accelerating its timeline for reducing asset purchases and raising interest rates, and has begun discussing balance sheet reduction. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy significantly, global financial conditions could also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt-servicing capacity, and disorderly capital outflows could exert pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could expose global commodity prices to continued upward pressure, exacerbating shortages in industrial supplies and increasing financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 examines whether swing pricing—a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds—can reduce these funds' liquidity risk during periods of market stress and discusses the tool's potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, although the recovery momentum in some Southeast Asian economies slowed temporarily in the third quarter due to the reimposition of strict pandemic control measures, while technology-product exporting economies in the region (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although markets generally expect a broad-based recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, the region's short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new virus variants remain a concern, especially for economies with lower vaccination rates and limited public health resources. Second, faster policy normalisation by the Federal Reserve could trigger capital outflows from the region and exacerbate currency depreciation pressures; economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support economic recovery will face more difficult trade-offs between curbing capital outflows and supporting economic activity. Third, a slowdown in major economies, coupled with a potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on trade growth prospects. Fourth, the rise in prices of various commodities triggered by the conflict between Russia and Ukraine will feed through to regional inflation and simultaneously weaken consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the decision-making process for monetary policy normalisation by regional central banks will become more complex. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the long run, to rebuild a sustainable and robust growth model, investors will need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 studies the sensitivity of stock returns to changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by firms' environmental performance. Economic growth in mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures, and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the short term due to the continued weakness in the property market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant. As a result, the mainland authorities have made stabilising growth a top priority for the year and have introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. Both the total amount of onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises decreased in the second half of 2021; Box 3 discusses whether the pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. The overall risk in the banking sector remains controllable, as mainland banks (especially systemically important banks) have limited exposure to loans to property developers, low non-performing loan ratios, and high provision coverage ratios. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, although at a slower pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew moderately, benefiting from the continued recovery of the global economy, improvements in the local labour market, and the government's consumption voucher scheme, which supported merchandise exports and private consumption. On a year-on-year basis, the economy grew by 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For the full year of 2021, the economy grew by 6.4%, marking the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local pandemic outbreaks and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures have put pressure on economic activity in Hong Kong. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-Epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Guaranteed Personal Loan Scheme" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" were enhanced, with maximum loan amounts increased and application and repayment periods extended. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with the banking industry, also extended the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" until the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year option to repay part of the principal, which also applies to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme". Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue its recovery for the full year of 2022, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting a slowdown in global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The government's promotion of various public works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The government forecasts that real GDP will grow by 2.0% to 3.5% in 2022, while the average growth forecast from international organisations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery will be affected by the uncertainties and risks discussed in previous sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% at the end of the year. Overall employment rebounded but remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data showed that labour market pressures re-emerged amid a new wave of local pandemic outbreaks. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. A new wave of local pandemic outbreaks and tightened pandemic control measures will put some pressure on the local labour market in the short term, especially in industries involving face-to-face contact. In the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on the development of the local pandemic and the pace of the local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have increased somewhat in recent months but remain moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate rose slightly to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The underlying inflation rate, measured on a three-month moving average annualised basis, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months, partly due to rising prices for dining out and some energy-related items. Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the short term as import prices increase and logistics are disrupted by the pandemic. However, weak rental growth and moderate local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast for overall inflation in 2022 is 2.4%, while the government expects overall inflation in 2022 to be 2.1% and underlying inflation to be 2.0%. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually weakened against the US dollar amid risk aversion in the local stock market. Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021, its upward momentum subsequently faded, mainly due to weak net inflows of southbound funds through Stock Connect (Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong) and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve normalises its monetary policy. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar remained in the strong side of the convertibility undertaking range for most of the time, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately over the review period, with no significant signs of funds flowing out of the Hong Kong banking system. Trading in Hong Kong's interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. Given ample interbank liquidity, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) remained low during the review period. The average lending rate for new mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Offshore renminbi banking business continued to thrive. In particular, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi funding pool continued to grow, with renminbi customer deposits and certificate of deposit balances increasing to RMB 1,113.5 billion as of the end of January 2022. Although renminbi loan balances decreased, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. The average daily transaction volume of the Renminbi Real-time Gross Settlement System rose to RMB 1,522.6 billion in 2021. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from Hong Kong's efficient financial infrastructure, the two-way Stock Connect (Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong), Bond Connect, and the Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening of the mainland's capital account, increased demand for renminbi assets from international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives. Fueled by government monetary and fiscal stimulus, the global economic recovery, and strong corporate earnings, major global stock markets generally continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, with the MSCI World Index reaching a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022. However, growing concerns about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid surging inflation risks, sharp rises in commodity prices, and escalating Russia-Ukraine tensions have led to a consolidation in major global stock markets since early January 2022.

Due to the rapid global spread of COVID-19 variants (Delta and Omicron) and persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed significantly in late 2021, with growth momentum remaining weak into 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and broadened across a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Heightened inflation concerns prompted a hawkish shift in the Federal Reserve's monetary policy stance, exacerbating the risk that a premature tightening of global financial conditions could put pressure on currently elevated asset valuations and hinder recovery in emerging markets, where progress remains uneven. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has driven up energy and other commodity prices, triggered volatility in global financial markets, and intensified some of these risks. In emerging Asia, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021 despite the spread of the Delta variant, with major technology-exporting economies in the region continuing to outperform others. While the Omicron variant is not expected to severely disrupt the region's economic recovery, any uncertainty related to new variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region's economic outlook. Additionally, the Federal Reserve's policy normalization could trigger asset price adjustments in the region, while slower growth in major economies could weigh on the region's merchandise export growth. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine will not only drive up commodity prices and increase inflation risks, but will also weaken consumption and heighten global economic uncertainty, complicating the monetary policy normalization decisions of regional central banks. In mainland China, economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021 due to a resurgence of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing, and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from a cooling property market and Omicron outbreaks. In view of this, the government has made stabilizing growth a top priority for the year, and macroeconomic policies are expected to provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed markedly in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of Delta, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tighter restrictions on movement worldwide. In addition, supply chain issues, such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs like semiconductors, continued to constrain output. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the United States and other major advanced economies, and slower growth momentum in mainland China offsetting an expected rebound in other parts of Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF Real GDP Growth Projections. Amid slowing global economic growth, inflationary pressures continued to build during the review period. Core inflation (which excludes food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, particularly in the United States, which had implemented larger-scale policy stimulus since the pandemic began. Amid supply bottlenecks, pent-up demand being released, and labor shortages, inflationary pressures have broadened across a wide range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has driven up prices for a range of commodities, which could exacerbate already elevated global inflationary pressures.
